title: The Akathist
hook: a Byzantine hymn to Mary sung standing

segments.voice: Yesterday, the oldest Marian prayer, the Sub tuum praesidium: people running for cover together. Your line was we fly to thee.

Here's a hymn whose name is an instruction about chairs. In the Byzantine churches, the Orthodox and the Eastern Catholic churches, there's a long hymn to Mary that nobody sits down for. Its name, the Akathist, means not sitting. The church fills, the singing starts, and the people stay on their feet, stanza after stanza, while one greeting comes around again and again: rejoice. A story people tell says it was once sung through a whole night, standing, by a city giving thanks for being saved from a siege. Whatever its history, the posture stuck.
screen: `A HYMN NAMED FOR NOT SITTING.` → `THE PEOPLE STAY ON THEIR FEET.` → `REJOICE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Akathistos, in Greek, means not seated. Standing is what a person does when someone they honor walks into the room, and the hymn makes that a whole service: the body says what the words are saying. Some people stand to show respect; some stand because they can't sit still with joy. This hymn asks for both. Then the greeting. The word that keeps returning is chaire, rejoice, or hail. It's the angel's word. In Luke's Gospel, Gabriel opens with it, which the Douay-Rheims renders "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." The Akathist multiplies that one greeting, line after line, each rejoice hung with a new picture of Mary, the way the Litany of Loreto stacks its names. At the end of each long stanza comes the refrain: rejoice, unwedded bride. Then the story underneath. The hymn doesn't only praise; it walks through the Gospel. Gabriel's visit. The birth. The shepherds. The magi following the star. The rejoices rise out of the story, like applause at each turn of a play. Last, where it lives. Eastern churches sing it especially in Lent, and that includes the Byzantine Catholic churches, in full communion with Rome. For a Latin Catholic, it's a reminder that the Church breathes, in a phrase Pope John Paul the Second used, with two lungs, East and West. The same Mary, the same angel's word, said in a different key, and on your feet.
screen: `AKATHISTOS: NOT SEATED.` · `CHAIRE: THE ANGEL'S WORD.` · `THE GOSPEL STORY UNDERNEATH.` · `EAST AND WEST, TWO LUNGS.` · then, large: `REJOICE, UNWEDDED BRIDE.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand up now; if you can't, sit up tall and let that be your standing, feet steady, shoulders loose, the way you'd straighten if someone had just walked in. If you pray, say the angel's greeting, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, or the refrain, rejoice, unwedded bride, once with each slow breath. If you don't, simply stand in honor of someone you love, and let your body say it.
The Akathist. A Byzantine hymn to Mary, its name meaning not seated: a chain of rejoices, built on the angel's greeting and the Gospel story, sung on your feet.
Your line: sung standing. The body says what the words are saying. On your feet, and see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians sing the Akathist to the Mother of God standing, especially in Lent, and some pray it at home or in shorter parts through the week.

chat.says: Why does everyone stand the whole time for the Akathist hymn?
options: Its name means not seated: people stand the way they would when someone they honor walks in.
Standing is a penance for Lent, meant to make the long hymn as tiring as possible.
It's a rule from the siege: soldiers stood guard while singing, and nobody may sit since.
chat.meaning: Akathistos means not seated. Standing honors someone who enters, so the body says what the hymn's rejoices are saying.

notes: The meaning of the name (akathistos, 'not seated') is stated; it is the standard sense of the Greek and the source of the index carry 'sung standing'. Confirm under the claims rule.
The siege story (traditionally the deliverance of Constantinople) is told only as 'a story people tell', without naming the city, date or enemy.
Claim that the hymn's first part walks through the Gospel story (Annunciation, Nativity, shepherds, magi); confirm.
Refrain rendered 'rejoice, unwedded bride' (Greek Χαῖρε, Νύμφη ἀνύμφευτε); the English is the script's own. Confirm.
'Especially in Lent' (the Saturday of the Akathist and Lenten Fridays in Byzantine use); stated without counts. Confirm.
'Two lungs' image is attributed to John Paul II (Ut Unum Sint 54; also elsewhere); paraphrased. Confirm reference.
Practice repeats the angel's greeting as a prayer line; no new prayer written.
